name: DOE-1 Sessions 2 - E-Commerce Data Organization and Retrival.docx
text:
Session 2: Search Techniques in E-Commerce and Tree Based Indexing Systems

Session Description

Searching is at the heart of every e-commerce platform. When a customer types a product name into a search bar, the system must return relevant results in milliseconds — even when the catalogue contains millions of items. This session explores the core searching algorithms used in such systems. Students study linear search (sequential scanning), binary search (divide and conquer on sorted data), and a brief introduction to informed search methods such as heuristic-guided search. 

Building on the BST concepts from Session 2, this session focuses on advanced tree structures used for production-grade indexing in e-commerce. While a simple BST works well on balanced data, it can degrade to O(n) performance when data is inserted in sorted order. AVL trees solve this by maintaining balance automatically through rotations. Students implement both a BST and an AVL tree, insert the same product dataset into both, and observe how the height (and therefore search time) differs. They also explore how B-trees — a generalisation used in databases — allow multiple keys per node, making them highly efficient for disk-based storage of millions of product records.

The practical component connects theory to industry: students trace how a real database index (like those used in MySQL or PostgreSQL) uses tree structures to speed up SQL queries on product tables, relating abstract concepts to tools they will encounter in professional practice.


Student Tasks

What your team must do in Session 2
1
Implement linear search and binary search in Python on a sorted list of at least 50 product names; record and compare execution times for 10 different queries. Analyse the best-case, average-case, and worst-case time complexity of linear and binary search using Big-O notation and provide worked examples from your dataset.
2
Design a simple indexing system using a Python dictionary that maps product categories to lists of products and demonstrate faster retrieval compared to a linear scan. Compare at least three real-world search tools (e.g., Amazon search, Flipkart search, Google Shopping) and identify which algorithmic principles they likely employ.
3
Implement a BST and an AVL tree in Python; insert the same 20 products in sorted order and compare the resulting tree heights and search depths. Demonstrate at least one AVL rotation (left-rotate or right-rotate) with a hand-drawn diagram showing the before and after state of the tree.
4
Research and document how B-trees differ from binary trees and explain why B-trees are preferred in relational database indexing. Write a Python function to perform in-order traversal of your AVL tree and verify that it returns products in sorted order (e.g., by price).
5
Scrapbook: Document search algorithm pseudocode, complexity analysis, and a reflection on how indexing reduces search time. Include diagrams of BST vs. AVL tree for the same dataset, rotation diagrams, and a summary of B-tree use cases.







Learning Targets

What is the difference between linear search and binary search in terms of time complexity and use cases?
Why must data be sorted before binary search can be applied, and what is the cost of sorting?
How does an index (such as a dictionary or hash map) reduce the time needed to search a large dataset?
What does Big-O notation tell us about the scalability of a searching algorithm?
How do real-world e-commerce platforms handle search across millions of products in near real time?
Why does inserting sorted data into a BST cause performance degradation, and how does an AVL tree prevent this?
What are tree rotations and how do they restore the balance property of an AVL tree?
How does tree height relate to worst-case search time, and why is minimising height important?
What is a B-tree and how does it extend the binary tree concept for use in databases?
How are tree-based indexes used in real database engines to speed up queries on large product tables?


Session Output

What to Submit at the End of Session 2
Scrapbook Entry: Pseudocode, complexity tables, and reflections for linear and binary search. Hand-drawn BST and AVL tree diagrams for the same dataset, with height labels. Array and tree diagrams for Min-Heap and Max-Heap after each insertion step.
Code Output: Python scripts demonstrating linear search, binary search, and dictionary-based indexing with timing comparisons. Python implementations of BST and AVL tree with insert, search, and in-order traversal; height comparison results. Python implementations of Min-Heap from scratch and heapq-based Max-Heap; priority queue for order fulfilment.
Complexity Analysis Table: Best, average, and worst-case time complexity for each algorithm with examples.
B-Tree Research Note: A concise written explanation (5–8 lines) of B-tree structure and its advantages for database indexing.
Complexity Comparison Table: Insert, extract, and peek operations for heap vs. sorted array vs. unsorted array.
Questions to Self: Each student writes 3–5 personal reflection questions.

name: DOE-1 Sessions 3 - E-Commerce Data Organization and Retrival.docx
text:
Session 3: Heap Structures for Priority Handling and Graph Based Recommended Systems


Session Description

In e-commerce, products are constantly being ranked and re-ranked - by price, ratings, discount percentage, popularity, or delivery speed. Heap data structures provide an efficient mechanism for maintaining a partially ordered collection that always gives instant access to the highest- or lowest-priority item. This session covers Min-Heaps (the smallest element is always at the root, useful for finding the cheapest product) and Max-Heaps (the largest element is at the root, useful for finding the top-rated product). Students implement both using Python's heapq module and by building a heap from scratch to understand the underlying array representation. 

Recommendation engines are one of the most commercially valuable components of any e-commerce platform. This session introduces graphs as a data structure, covering vertices (users and products), edges (interactions such as views, purchases, or ratings), directed vs. undirected edges, and weighted edges (strength of association). Students model a small e-commerce dataset as a graph and apply Breadth-First Search (BFS) to find products within a certain degree of connection from a starting product.

Students also explore Depth-First Search (DFS) for traversing deeper relationship chains (e.g., users who bought A also bought B, and users who bought B also bought C). By implementing both traversals and analysing their outputs, students gain a concrete understanding of how recommendation logic works at the algorithmic level.


Student Tasks

What your team must do in Session 3
1
Implement a Min-Heap from scratch in Python using an array and support insert and extract-min operations; test it on a dataset of at least 15 products sorted by price.
2
Use Python's heapq module to implement a Max-Heap simulation (negate values) for the same dataset and rank products by rating in descending order.
3
Design a priority queue for an order fulfilment system where orders with the earliest delivery deadline are processed first; implement and test with at least 10 sample orders.
4
Compare the time complexity of heap operations (insert, extract, peek) with those of a sorted array and an unsorted array.
5
Model a dataset of 8 users and 12 products as a graph using an adjacency list in Python; edges represent purchase or view events.
6
Implement BFS from a given product node and return all products within 2 degrees of connection — these are the 'recommended products'.
7
Implement DFS from a given user node to discover all products reachable through the user-product-user chain and compare the output to BFS.
8
Add weights to edges (e.g., number of purchases) and modify your BFS to prioritise strongly connected products in the recommendation list.
9
Scrapbook: Document heap diagrams (array and tree representations), pseudocode, complexity tables, and reflections on real-world applications. Include the graph diagram, adjacency list, BFS and DFS traversal outputs, and a written reflection on how edge weights improve recommendation quality.

Learning Targets

What is the heap property and how do Min-Heap and Max-Heap differ?
How is a heap represented as an array, and how do parent-child index relationships work?
Why do heap insert and extract operations run in O(log n) time?
What is a priority queue and how does it differ from a standard queue?
How can heaps be applied in e-commerce to handle product ranking, order scheduling, or flash-sale inventory management?
What is a graph, and how do vertices and edges represent users and products in an e-commerce context?
What is the difference between BFS and DFS, and when is each more appropriate for recommendation tasks?
How do weighted edges improve the accuracy of a recommendation system compared to unweighted graphs?
What is the time complexity of BFS and DFS on a graph with V vertices and E edges?
How do real-world recommendation engines such as collaborative filtering relate to graph-based traversal algorithms?


Session Output

What to Submit at the End of Session 3
Scrapbook Entry: Array and tree diagrams for Min-Heap and Max-Heap after each insertion step. Hand-drawn or digital graph diagram with adjacency list and BFS/DFS traversal traces.
Code Output: Python implementations of Min-Heap from scratch and heapq-based Max-Heap; priority queue for order fulfilment. Python graph implementation with BFS and DFS traversal; weighted recommendation output.
Complexity Comparison Table: Insert, extract, and peek operations for heap vs. sorted array vs. unsorted array.
Recommendation Output: A list of the top 5 recommended products for a given starting user or product, with justification.
Questions to Self: Each student writes 3–5 personal reflection questions.

name: DOE-1 Sessions 4 - E-Commerce Data Organization and Retrival.docx
text:
SESSION 4: Hashing for Fast Lookup

Session Description

When a user searches for a product by its ID, or when the system needs to verify whether a username already exists, the operation must complete in near-constant time regardless of how large the database has grown. Hash tables make this possible by mapping keys (product IDs, usernames) to memory locations using a hash function, enabling O(1) average-case lookups.

This session covers the design of hash functions, the concept of load factor, and the two primary collision resolution strategies: chaining (each bucket holds a linked list of entries) and open addressing (probing for the next available slot). Students implement both strategies and test them with real product datasets to observe the effect of collisions on performance.

Students also explore Python dictionaries as a built-in hash table implementation and use them to build a product lookup system, a username-to-profile mapping, and a frequency counter for search terms - three of the most common real-world applications of hashing in e-commerce.

Student Tasks

What your team must do in Session 4
1
Design and implement a simple hash function for string keys (product names); analyse its distribution by inserting 20 products and counting collisions.
2
Implement a hash table with chaining (linked list per bucket) and one with open addressing (linear probing); test both with the same dataset and compare collision rates.
3
Build a product lookup system using a Python dictionary that maps product IDs to product records and supports O(1) insert, search, and delete.
4
Implement a search-term frequency counter using a hash map that records how many times each search term has been queried; output the top 5 most-searched terms.
5
Scrapbook: Document hash function design, collision examples, code snippets, and a reflection on when chaining vs. open addressing is preferable.

Learning Targets

What is a hash function and what properties must it have to distribute keys evenly?
What is a collision in a hash table, and how do chaining and open addressing resolve it differently?
Why is the load factor important, and how does it affect hash table performance?
What is the average-case and worst-case time complexity of hash table operations, and under what conditions does worst case occur?
How are Python dictionaries implemented under the hood, and why are they so efficient for lookups?


Session Output

What to Submit at the End of Session 4
Scrapbook Entry: Hash function design, collision diagrams for chaining and open addressing, and load-factor analysis.
Code Output: Python implementations of hash table with chaining and with open addressing; product lookup system; search-term frequency counter.
Collision Rate Table: Number of collisions for each resolution strategy across different load factors.
Questions to Self: Each student writes 3–5 personal reflection questions.

name: DOE-1 Sessions 5 - E-Commerce Data Organization and Retrival (1).docx
text:
SESSION 5: AI-Based Search Optimisation and Knowledge Reprasentation

Session Description

Classical search algorithms like BFS and DFS explore search spaces exhaustively, which becomes impractical for large, complex e-commerce scenarios such as personalised product ranking or dynamic pricing. Informed search algorithms use heuristics - problem-specific knowledge - to guide exploration towards the most promising solutions first, dramatically reducing the search space. The session also briefly explores game-based search (Minimax with alpha-beta pruning) as a framework for understanding adversarial optimisation - for example, dynamic pricing where a retailer and a competitor each try to optimise their price. While full implementation is optional, the conceptual mapping to e-commerce strategy is discussed and documented.

This session introduces three Knowledge Representation (KR) technologies applicable to e-commerce: semantic networks (graphs where nodes are concepts and edges are relationships like 'is-a' and 'has-part'), frames (structured records that bundle an object's attributes and default values - similar to a class in object-oriented programming), and production rules (IF-THEN rules that trigger actions based on conditions, used in recommendation engines and fraud detection). Students apply these techniques to represent a small product catalogue, a user preference profile, and a set of discount rules. They then write a simple rule-based inference engine in Python that applies production rules to a user's cart and outputs personalised discount recommendations - a simplified but realistic model of the rule engines used by major e-commerce platforms.


Student Tasks

What your team must do in Session 5
1
Define a heuristic function h(n) for product search that estimates the relevance of a product node to a given user query based on price, rating, and category match score. Create a semantic network (using NetworkX or a hand-drawn diagram) for at least 15 product concepts showing 'is-a', 'has-part', 'used-with', and 'similar-to' relationships.
2
Implement greedy best-first search using a priority queue (from Session 5) to return the top 5 products ranked by your heuristic; compare results to a random ordering. Design frame structures for three product categories (e.g., Laptop, Running Shoes, Cookware) including slots for attributes, data types, default values, and constraints.
3
Implement A* search for the same product space using f(n) = g(n) + h(n), where g(n) is a relevance cost based on number of filtering steps applied. Write a set of at least 8 IF-THEN production rules for a discount recommendation system (e.g., IF cart_total > 1000 AND category == 'Electronics' THEN apply 10% discount).
4
Compare the number of nodes explored by BFS (Session 6), greedy best-first, and A* for the same query; document the trade-off between completeness and efficiency. Implement a Python rule engine that evaluates a sample user cart against your production rules and outputs all applicable discounts in priority order.
5
Scrapbook: Include heuristic function definition, A* search trace, node-count comparison table, and a conceptual note on Minimax in dynamic pricing. Include the semantic network diagram, frame designs, full rule set, rule engine code, and a reflection on the advantages of rule-based systems over hard-coded logic.




Learning Targets

What is an informed search algorithm and how does a heuristic function guide it?
How can the product-search problem be formulated as a state-space search with nodes, edges, and a goal state?
What is Minimax search and how might it apply conceptually to competitive pricing strategies in e-commerce?
What is Knowledge Representation and why is it important for building intelligent e-commerce systems?
What is a frame structure and how does it resemble an object-oriented class definition?
How do production rules (IF-THEN) enable automated reasoning and recommendation in e-commerce platforms?
What are the trade-offs between rule-based systems and machine-learning-based approaches for product recommendation?


Session Output

What to Submit at the End of Session 5
Scrapbook Entry: Node-count comparison across BFS and greedy. Frame designs, full production rule set, and rule engine output.
Code Output: Python implementations of greedy best-first search for product recommendation; comparison output. Python rule engine that evaluates a sample cart and returns personalised discount recommendations.
Reflection Note: A concise written explanation (5–8 lines) of how informed search reduces unnecessary computation compared to uninformed BFS. A concise written explanation (5–8 lines) comparing the expressiveness and scalability of the three KR techniques.
Questions to Self: Each student writes 3–5 personal reflection questions.

name: DOE-1 Sessions 6 - E-Commerce Data Organization and Retrival.docx
text:
SESSION 6: Python Implementation (NumPy & Pandas)

Session Description

The algorithms and data structures studied in previous sessions work beautifully at small scale; but real e-commerce datasets contain millions of rows - millions of products, transactions, and user events. Implementing custom data structures for such scale is impractical. Python's NumPy and Pandas libraries provide highly optimised, vectorised operations that can process large datasets orders of magnitude faster than pure Python loops. Students load a realistic e-commerce CSV dataset (provided or self-sourced from Kaggle), perform exploratory data analysis, clean and filter the data, compute summary statistics, and apply sorting and grouping operations - all using Pandas DataFrames and NumPy arrays. The session closes with a visualisation task using matplotlib or seaborn, producing charts that communicate data insights relevant to business decisions.


Student Tasks

What your team must do in Session 6
1
Load a CSV dataset of at least 500 e-commerce product records into a Pandas DataFrame; inspect shape, data types, and missing values; clean and preprocess the data.
2
Filter products by price range, category, and minimum rating using Pandas boolean indexing; sort the results by price and by rating and compare outputs.
3
Compute summary statistics (mean, median, standard deviation, min, max) for price and rating columns across the full dataset and separately for each category.
4
Use groupby to aggregate sales data by category and month; identify the top 3 categories by total revenue and the top 5 products by number of orders.
5
Produce at least three visualisations (bar chart, histogram, scatter plot) using matplotlib or seaborn that communicate actionable insights from the dataset; include titles, axis labels, and a one-sentence business interpretation for each chart.


Learning Targets

How do NumPy arrays differ from Python lists in terms of memory layout and performance, and why does this matter for large datasets?
What is a Pandas DataFrame and how does it extend the concept of a 2D array with labelled columns and indices?
How does boolean indexing in Pandas implement the filtering logic studied in earlier sessions more efficiently?
What aggregation and grouping operations does Pandas provide, and how do they relate to SQL GROUP BY clauses?
How can data visualisation (charts and graphs) turn raw statistics into business insights for an e-commerce decision-maker?

















Session Output

What to Submit at the End of Session 6
Scrapbook Entry: Dataset description, data cleaning steps, key statistics, and interpretation of each visualisation.
Code Output: Fully annotated Jupyter Notebook (.ipynb) or Python script covering loading, cleaning, filtering, aggregation, and visualisation.
Visualisation Output: Three saved chart images (.png) with titles, axis labels, and business interpretations.
Questions to Self: Each student writes 3–5 personal reflection questions.

name: DOE-1 Sessions 7 - E-Commerce Data Organization and Retrival.docx
text:
SESSION 7: System Integration & Testing

Session Description

This session is dedicated to integrating these components into a single, coherent e-commerce data system and rigorously testing its behaviour. Integration is rarely straightforward - interfaces between modules must align, data formats must be consistent, and edge cases (empty catalogues, duplicate products, malformed queries) must be handled gracefully. Students refactor their code into well-named functions and modules, write integration tests, and conduct peer review sessions where another team evaluates their system against a set of defined test cases.


Student Tasks

What your team must do in Session 7
1
Refactor all previous code into a unified project structure with clearly named modules (e.g., catalog.py, search.py, recommend.py, analytics.py) and a main.py entry point.
2
Write at least 10 integration test cases covering: product insertion, deletion, search by name and by category, recommendation output, discount rule application, and data analytics summary.
3
Conduct a peer review session with another team: exchange your system and test cases; each team runs the other's tests, documents failures, and provides written feedback.
4
Measure and plot end-to-end query response time for catalogue sizes of 10, 100, 500, and 1,000 products; identify any operations that do not scale as expected and propose optimisations.
5
Scrapbook: Include the project structure diagram, all test cases and results, peer review feedback received and given, and the performance curve with interpretation.


Learning Targets

What is software integration and why does combining individually working modules sometimes produce unexpected failures?
What are integration tests and how do they differ from unit tests in terms of scope and purpose?
How does peer review improve software quality, and what makes constructive technical feedback effective?
How can empirical performance measurement complement theoretical Big-O analysis?
What refactoring strategies improve code readability, maintainability, and testability in a Python project?


Session Output

What to Submit at the End of Session 7
Scrapbook Entry: Project structure diagram, test cases with pass/fail results, peer review feedback summary, and performance curve.
Code Output: Fully integrated and refactored Python project with at least 10 integration tests; performance measurement script.
Peer Review Report: Written evaluation of the reviewed team's system (strengths, identified bugs, improvement suggestions) — 1 page per team.
Questions to Self: Each student writes 3–5 personal reflection questions.

name: DOE-1 Sessions 8 - E-Commerce Data Organization and Retrival.docx
text:
SESSION 8: Project Demonstration

Session Description

Session eight is the culmination of the entire semester. Each team presents their completed e-commerce data system to an audience of peers and instructors, demonstrating the full pipeline: efficient data organisation, fast retrieval, intelligent recommendations, rule-based discounting, and data analytics. The demonstration must be live - all features are shown running on real data, not pre-recorded or mocked.

The presentation is structured as a product pitch combined with a technical walkthrough. Teams explain the problem they were solving, justify their choice of data structures and algorithms at each stage, show the system handling real queries, and present the performance benchmarks from Session seven. Questions from the audience test the depth of understanding behind every design decision.


Student Tasks

What your team must do in Session 8
1
Prepare a 10–12 minute live demonstration covering: system overview, data structure choices (with justification), live search and recommendation queries, discount rule application, and analytics output.
2
Create a 1-page technical poster or slide deck (maximum 8 slides) summarising the system architecture, key algorithms used, performance benchmarks, and lessons learned.
3
Rehearse the demonstration at least twice before Session 8; all team members must be able to explain any component of the system if questioned by the audience.
4
Prepare answers to at least 5 likely technical questions (e.g., 'Why did you choose a hash table over a BST for product lookup?', 'How does your recommendation system handle a new user with no history?').
5
Submit the completed Scrapbook and a 300–500 word individual learning reflection covering growth across all 8 sessions and connection to future career goals.


Learning Targets

How do I communicate a complex technical system clearly and confidently to a mixed technical and non-technical audience?
How do all the data structures and algorithms covered in this project interconnect within a single coherent system?
What are the most significant design trade-offs made during the project, and how would I justify them under questioning?
How does building a full project from requirements to demonstration deepen understanding compared to isolated exercises?
What skills, habits, and ways of thinking developed in this project will transfer to future engineering courses and professional roles?







Session Output

What to Submit at the End of Session 8
Live Demonstration: Full system demo (10–12 minutes) with live queries, recommendation outputs, discount rules, and analytics — all on real data.
Technical Poster / Slide Deck: 1-page poster or maximum 8-slide deck covering architecture, algorithms, benchmarks, and lessons learned.
Completed Scrapbook: All entries from Sessions 1–8 compiled and submitted as a complete learning artefact.
